pos: noun (bereaved women under God's special care)
etymology: From the Old English widewe, akin to Latin vidua; women bereaved of their husbands, set in Scripture under the special protection of God and the duty of His people.
biblical_def: Widows are women bereaved of their husbands, whom Scripture places under the special protection of God and the particular care of His people. The LORD names Himself “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows”; He pleads their cause, defends them against oppression, and threatens His wrath upon those who afflict them. Pure religion before God, says James, is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction. The early church organized its mercy around this duty: when the widows of the Grecians were neglected in the daily ministration, the apostles appointed the seven, the seed of the diaconate, to serve the tables. Paul gives the church careful rule: honour widows that are widows indeed—the truly destitute and godly, who trust in God and continue in supplications—while charging families first to provide for their own, lest the church be burdened and natural duty neglected. The dictionary marks the care of widows as a non-negotiable mark of true religion and a chief work of the church's mercy, against two errors. The first is the neglect that leaves the bereaved to want while the church spends on itself—a neglect God Himself avenges. The second is the modern outsourcing of all such mercy to the state, as though the family and the church were relieved of a duty Scripture lays squarely upon them. God is the defender of widows; His people are His hands.
webster_summary: Women bereaved of their husbands, under God's special protection (Psalm 68:5) and the church's particular care (James 1:27; 1 Timothy 5:3); their relief a mark of pure religion, neglected at the peril of God's wrath.
webster_full: WIDOWS, noun. [Old English widewe.] Women bereaved of their husbands.
God is “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” (Psalm 68:5).
Pure religion visits the fatherless and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
The church is to honour widows that are widows indeed (1 Timothy 5:3).
The neglect of widows occasioned the appointing of the seven (Acts 6:1).
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Honour widows that are widows indeed.
A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
Ac 6:1
And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
corruption_summary: The church errs by neglecting widows while spending on itself; the modern age errs by outsourcing all such mercy to the state, as though family and church were relieved of a duty Scripture lays on them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care of widows as a mark of true religion. The first corruption is plain neglect—a church that spends on its own comfort while the bereaved among it want. God names this an offense He avenges, for He is the judge of the widows and hears the cry of the oppressed. The neglect of the Grecian widows nearly fractured the early church and forced the appointing of the seven; the dictionary holds the relief of widows to be a chief and non-negotiable work of the church's mercy.

The second and modern corruption is the outsourcing of all such mercy to the state, as though family and church were relieved of the duty by the welfare office. Scripture orders it otherwise: families are to provide first for their own widows, that the church be not charged; and the church is to honour and relieve those who are widows indeed. The dictionary recovers the layered biblical pattern—family, then church—against both the cold individualism that says “not my concern” and the lazy collectivism that says “let the government do it.” God is the defender of widows, and His people, not the bureaucracy, are appointed His hands.
roots_summary: From the Old English widewe and Latin vidua; the Hebrew 'almanah and Greek chera name the bereaved woman whom God defends and the church relieves.
roots_lines: Widewe, Old English, a widow, akin to Latin vidua (bereft).
'Almanah, Hebrew, a widow, one of the classes of the defenseless God protects.
Chera, Greek, a widow, the object of the church's ordered care (1 Timothy 5).
“Widows indeed” (Greek ontos chera), the truly destitute and godly widow.
The neglect of widows occasioned the diaconate (Acts 6:1-6).
usage: The deacons made the relief of widows a first charge, as the early church had done.
The pastor preached that to neglect the bereaved while spending on comfort is a sin God avenges.
She honoured the widow indeed, while urging the family to provide first for its own.

etymology: From the Authorized Version of Ezekiel 36:26; the soft, living, responsive heart God promises to give in place of the stony heart, the figure of regeneration.
biblical_def: The heart of flesh is the soft, living, responsive heart that God promises to give His people in the place of the stony heart—the great Old Testament figure of regeneration and the new covenant. By Ezekiel the LORD declares: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” The stony heart is the unregenerate heart—hard, dead, unfeeling toward God, unable to repent or believe; the heart of flesh is the renewed heart, made tender, alive, and obedient by the Spirit, on which the law of God is written. The promise belongs to the new covenant: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.” The dictionary marks the heart of flesh as a clear witness to monergistic regeneration: God Himself performs the surgery, taking away the stone and giving the flesh; the dead heart does not soften itself, for a stone cannot make itself supple. It marks the doctrine against the synergism that makes the sinner's own willing the cause of the new heart, when Scripture makes the new heart the cause of right willing. The heart of flesh is not the natural sentimentality the world prizes, nor mere emotional warmth; it is the Spirit-wrought tenderness toward God that grieves at sin, loves His law, and turns to Him in faith—the inward reality of which baptism is the sign and the new birth the cause.
webster_summary: The soft, living, responsive heart God gives in place of the stony heart (Ezekiel 36:26), the figure of regeneration and the new covenant; God Himself performs the surgery, a witness to monergistic new birth.
webster_full: HEART OF FLESH, noun phrase. The soft, living heart God gives in place of the stony heart.
“I will take away the stony heart… and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).
The figure of regeneration and the new covenant (Ezekiel 11:19).
On it the law of God is written (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3).
God performs the surgery; the dead stone cannot soften itself—monergistic new birth.
scriptures: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh:

Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
corruption_summary: Synergism makes the sinner's own willing the cause of the new heart; sentimentalism reduces the heart of flesh to mere emotional warmth. Both miss the Spirit-wrought, God-given regeneration the figure declares.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is monergistic regeneration. Synergism teaches that the sinner first softens his own heart, or cooperates to bring about the new birth; the new heart waits on the man's willing. Ezekiel forbids this: God takes away the stony heart and gives the heart of flesh. A stone cannot make itself supple, nor a dead man quicken himself. The new heart is the cause of right willing, not its effect; the surgery is God's, sovereign and effectual.

The opposite corruption, fed by the sentimental age, reduces the heart of flesh to mere emotional warmth or natural tenderness—a soft, feeling temperament the world admires. But the heart of flesh is not sentimentality; it is the Spirit-wrought renewal that grieves at sin, loves the law of God, and turns to Him in faith. The dictionary recovers the figure as the inward reality of the new covenant: a heart made alive and obedient by the Spirit, on which God writes His law—of which baptism is the outward sign and regeneration the inward cause.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew lev basar (“heart of flesh”) set against lev ha-'even (“the stony heart”) in Ezekiel; the figure of the regenerate heart of the new covenant.
roots_lines: Lev basar, Hebrew, “heart of flesh,” the soft, living, responsive heart.
Lev ha-'even, Hebrew, “the stony heart,” the hard, dead, unregenerate heart.
Ruach chadashah, “a new spirit,” given with the new heart (Ezekiel 36:26).
Paralleled by the law written on “fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3).
A new-covenant promise (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 11:19).
usage: The pastor preached the heart of flesh to show that God alone removes the stone and gives the new heart.
He answered the synergist: a stone cannot soften itself, nor a dead man quicken himself.
She distinguished the Spirit-wrought tender heart from the world's mere sentimentality.

etymology: From the Latin maturitas, ripeness; in Scripture, the full-growth of the believer who has passed from spiritual infancy to the stature of a man in Christ.
biblical_def: Maturity is spiritual full-growth—the believer's passage from infancy to the stature of a man in Christ, marked by discernment, stability, and conformity to the Son of God. Scripture distinguishes babes in Christ, who can take only milk, from the of-full-age, to whom strong meat belongs, “even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.” The goal of the ministry of the Word is that we all come “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ,” no more children tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine. Paul labours to present every man perfect in Christ Jesus, and the apostle who once spake as a child put away childish things when he became a man. The dictionary marks maturity as the proper aim of the Christian life and of the church's teaching, against two errors. The first is the perpetual spiritual infancy that never grows—believers content to remain babes, unskilful in the word of righteousness, ever needing milk. The second is the false maturity that mistakes mere age, knowledge, or experience for ripeness; true maturity is not the accumulation of facts but the exercised discernment of good and evil and the increasing likeness to Christ. Maturity is grown, not granted in a moment: by the diligent use of the means of grace, the Word, prayer, the ordinances, and the fellowship of the saints, the babe is brought by the Spirit toward the fulness of Christ.
webster_summary: Spiritual full-growth—the believer's passage from infancy to the stature of Christ, marked by exercised discernment and stability (Hebrews 5:14; Ephesians 4:13); the aim of the Christian life, against perpetual infancy and false, merely-aged maturity.
webster_full: MATURITY, noun. [Latin maturitas, ripeness.] Spiritual full-growth in Christ.
Strong meat belongs to the of-full-age, with senses exercised to discern good and evil (Hebrews 5:14).
The aim: a perfect man, the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).
The mature put away childish things (1 Corinthians 13:11).
Grown by the diligent use of the means of grace, not granted in a moment.
scriptures: Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Eph 4:13
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:
When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: One error is the perpetual spiritual infancy that never grows past milk; the other is the false maturity that mistakes mere age, knowledge, or experience for the exercised discernment and Christlikeness Scripture means.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is growth toward the fulness of Christ as the aim of the Christian life. One corruption is perpetual infancy: believers content to remain babes, taking only milk, unskilful in the word of righteousness, never exercising their senses to discern good and evil. The writer to the Hebrews rebukes it—those who by reason of time ought to be teachers still need to be taught the first principles. The dictionary holds that the normal Christian life is one of real growth, not arrested development.

The opposite corruption is a false maturity that mistakes mere age, accumulated knowledge, or long experience for ripeness. A man may know much doctrine and have many years in the church and yet remain immature—unstable, undiscerning, unlike Christ. Scripture measures maturity not by facts stored but by senses exercised to discern good and evil and by the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ. The dictionary recovers maturity as a Spirit-wrought conformity to the Son, grown through the diligent use of the means of grace—the Word, prayer, the ordinances, and the communion of the saints.
roots_summary: From the Latin maturitas (ripeness); the Greek teleios (“perfect, full-grown”) and teleioi (“them that are of full age”) name the mature believer.
roots_lines: Maturitas, Latin, ripeness, from maturus, ripe.
Teleios, Greek, perfect or full-grown, the “perfect man” of Ephesians 4:13.
Teleioi, “them that are of full age” (Hebrews 5:14), against the babes.
Nepios, Greek, an infant or babe, the immature believer on milk.
Grown through the means of grace toward the fulness of Christ.
usage: The pastor pressed the church past milk toward strong meat and exercised discernment.
He warned that long years and much knowledge are not maturity without likeness to Christ.
She sought to grow by the means of grace toward the measure of the stature of Christ.

pos: noun (the singing of psalms in worship)
etymology: From the Greek psalmodia, the singing of psalms; the practice of singing the Psalms and other sacred song in the worship of God.
biblical_def: Psalmody is the singing of psalms—and, in the broader sense, of sacred song—in the worship of God, a duty commanded throughout Scripture and a chief part of the church's praise. The apostle bids the church speak “to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord,” and again, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” James directs the merry to sing psalms, and the Psalter itself opens the worship of God's people with the call, “O come, let us sing unto the LORD.” The dictionary holds psalmody to be a commanded element of worship and honours the high place of the inspired Psalms, the church's God-given hymnbook, which Christ Himself sang. Reformed Christians have differed on the question of exclusive psalmody—whether only the canonical Psalms may be sung, or whether uninspired hymns of sound doctrine are also lawful—and the dictionary does not bind the conscience on that disputed point, holding both the exclusive-psalmody position and the broader position to lie within the Reformed family. What it does mark is the abiding standard the regulative principle supplies: worship-song must be sung to the Lord, in the people's understanding, governed by the Word, and rich in the truth of God, against the sentimental, man-centred, and doctrinally vacant song that has flooded modern worship. Whether psalms only or psalms and faithful hymns, the church's song is to teach and admonish, to make melody in the heart, and to render the praise of God in the beauties of holiness.
webster_summary: The singing of psalms (and sacred song) in the worship of God (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19); a commanded element of worship, honouring the inspired Psalter, with the exclusive-psalmody question left within the Reformed family.
webster_full: PSALMODY, noun. [Greek psalmodia.] The singing of psalms and sacred song in worship.
Commanded: “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs… to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16).
“Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (James 5:13).
The inspired Psalter is the church's God-given hymnbook, which Christ sang.
The exclusive-psalmody question is left within the Reformed family.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Jas 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
corruption_summary: The flood of sentimental, man-centred, doctrinally vacant worship-song corrupts psalmody; the dictionary holds the regulative standard while leaving the exclusive-psalmody question open within the Reformed family.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is worship-song governed by the Word and rich in truth. The live corruption is the modern flood of sentimental, repetitive, man-centred song—music that exalts feeling over truth, the self over God, and emotional experience over doctrine. Against it the dictionary sets the apostolic standard: the church's song is to teach and admonish, dwelling richly in the word of Christ, making melody in the heart to the Lord. The recovery of the Psalter—the inspired hymnbook full of the whole counsel of God, including its laments and imprecations the age has lost—is a chief remedy.

On the disputed question, the dictionary keeps the Reformed family's liberty. Some hold to exclusive psalmody, that only the canonical Psalms may be sung in worship, since these alone are inspired and warranted; others hold that uninspired hymns of sound doctrine are also lawful under the regulative principle. The dictionary does not bind the conscience here, honouring both as Reformed. What it binds is the standard itself: whatever is sung must be sung to the Lord, intelligibly, governed by the Word, and full of the truth of God—never the vacant and self-centred song the regulative principle of worship excludes.
roots_summary: From the Greek psallo (to pluck a string, to sing praise) and psalmos (a psalm); whence psalmodia, the singing of psalms, and the Psalter, the church's sung praise.
roots_lines: Psallo, Greek, to pluck a string, hence to sing praise to God.
Psalmos, Greek, a psalm, a song sung to accompaniment.
Psalmodia, the singing of psalms, the root of “psalmody.”
The Psalter, the inspired hymnbook of the church, sung by Christ Himself.
Governed by the regulative principle of worship.
usage: The church recovered psalmody, singing the inspired Psalms with their laments the age had lost.
The pastor held both exclusive psalmody and the broader position to be within the Reformed family.
She judged worship-song by the apostolic standard: sung to the Lord, intelligible, full of truth.

etymology: Greek agathos, “good” — good in nature and in effect, beneficent; one of the New Testament's chief words for the good that belongs first to God and flows from Him to His works.
biblical_def: Agathos is the chief Greek adjective for “good” in the New Testament—good in its nature and beneficent in its effect, the good that does good. Its first and proper application is to God Himself: when the rich young ruler called Jesus “Good Master,” the Lord answered, “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God,” teaching that essential goodness belongs to God alone, and pressing the man to reckon with the deity of the One he addressed. From God, the fountain of good, goodness flows to His works and to His people: believers are “created in Christ Jesus unto good works (erga agatha), which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them,” and are called to overcome evil with good and to do good unto all men, especially the household of faith. The dictionary marks agathos as a witness to two truths. First, that all true goodness derives from God; the creature has no goodness of its own, and the natural man, however moral by human reckoning, is not agathos in the absolute sense, for none is good but God. Second, that the good works of the believer are real, necessary, and God-ordained—not the ground of salvation, for they are the fruit and not the root, but the appointed walk of those whom grace has made new. The dictionary marks the word against the moralism that calls fallen man good apart from God, and against the antinomianism that, prizing grace, despises the good works grace was given to produce.
webster_summary: The chief New Testament Greek word for “good” — good in nature and beneficent in effect; applied first to God alone (Matthew 19:17), then to the God-ordained good works of His people (Ephesians 2:10).
webster_full: AGATHOS, adjective. [Greek, “good.”] Good in nature and beneficent in effect; the good that does good.
Applied first to God: “there is none good but one, that is, God” (Matthew 19:17).
Believers are created unto good works (erga agatha) ordained by God (Ephesians 2:10).
We are to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21) and do good to all (Galatians 6:10).
All true goodness derives from God, the fountain of good.
scriptures: And he said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God: but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments.
Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
corruption_summary: Moralism calls fallen man “good” apart from God, against Christ's “none good but God”; antinomianism, prizing grace, despises the good works grace was given to produce.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all goodness derives from God. The moralism of the age calls fallen man basically good, measuring goodness by human kindness apart from God. The Lord's word to the young ruler corrects it: “there is none good but one, that is, God.” Essential goodness belongs to God alone; the creature's goodness is derived and, in the natural man fallen, corrupted at the root. To call man agathos in the absolute sense is to forget the fall and to flatter the sinner the gospel came to save.

The opposite corruption is the antinomianism that, rightly prizing grace, wrongly despises the good works grace produces. But believers are “created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained.” The dictionary holds the balance: good works are not the ground of salvation—they are fruit, not root—yet they are real, necessary, and God-ordained, the appointed walk of the redeemed. The grace that saves apart from works saves unto works; and the believer, made new, overcomes evil with good and does good to all men, especially the household of faith, returning the goodness that flows first from God.
roots_summary: From the Greek agathos (good, beneficent), distinguished from kalos (good as beautiful or fitting); the good that is good in itself and good in its working.
roots_lines: Agathos, Greek, good in nature and beneficent in effect.
Distinguished from kalos, good as beautiful, noble, or fitting.
Erga agatha, “good works,” ordained by God for His people (Ephesians 2:10).
Agathosune, the cognate noun “goodness,” a fruit of the Spirit.
Applied absolutely to God alone: “none good but one” (Matthew 19:17).
usage: The teacher showed from agathos that essential goodness belongs to God alone.
He preached that grace saves apart from works yet saves unto the good works God ordained.
She overcame evil with good, doing good to all, especially the household of faith.

etymology: From “plain” (Latin planus, flat, clear) and “speech”; the honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands — yea meaning yea, and nay meaning nay.
biblical_def: Plain speech is the honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands of His people: “Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” James repeats it: “Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.” The teaching forbids the manipulative oath-taking, the evasive equivocation, and the doubled and slippery word by which men deceive while keeping the letter of truth; the disciple's bare word is to be as binding as another man's oath, because he speaks in the presence of God who hates lying lips and delights in them that deal truly. Paul appeals to the same standard: “as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay”—not double, not shifting. The dictionary marks plain speech against the whole craft of deceitful communication: the flattery that says what it does not mean, the spin that technically avoids a lie while intending one, the broken promise dressed in fine words, and the mental reservation that betrays trust. It is not bluntness for its own sake, nor the rudeness that wounds under cover of “just being honest”; plain speech is truthful speech spoken in love, simple and reliable. The man of plain speech can be trusted on his word alone, for he reckons that he answers to God for every idle word, and that whatsoever exceeds the simple truth cometh of evil.
webster_summary: The honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands — yea meaning yea, nay meaning nay (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12); the bare word as binding as an oath, against equivocation, spin, and the deceitful doubled word.
webster_full: PLAIN SPEECH, noun phrase. Honest, simple, truthful speech.
“Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Matthew 5:37).
“Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay” (James 5:12).
The disciple's bare word is as binding as an oath, spoken before God.
Against equivocation, spin, flattery, and the deceitful doubled word.
scriptures: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.
corruption_summary: The age corrupts plain speech with spin, equivocation, and the technically-true lie; the opposite error is the rudeness that wounds under cover of “just being honest.”
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the binding truthfulness of the simple word. The age has perfected the craft of saying what is technically true while intending to deceive—spin, equivocation, the doubled and slippery word, the promise worded to be broken, the flattery that means nothing. The Lord forbids it all: let your yea be yea. The disciple's bare word is to be as reliable as another man's sworn oath, for he speaks before the God who hates lying lips and delights in them that deal truly; whatsoever exceeds the simple truth cometh of evil.

The opposite corruption hides cruelty behind candor—the rudeness that wounds and excuses itself with “I'm just being honest.” Plain speech is not bluntness for its own sake nor a license to bludgeon. It is truthful speech spoken in love, simple and trustworthy. The dictionary holds both edges: against the deceiver, the word must be true and reliable; against the brawler, the true word must be seasoned with grace. The man of plain speech can be trusted on his word alone, and he speaks that truth not to wound but to edify, knowing he answers to God for every word.
roots_summary: From the Latin planus (flat, clear) and the Lord's command of the simple “yea” and “nay”; truthful speech that needs no oath to be believed.
roots_lines: Planus, Latin, flat, level, clear—the root of “plain.”
“Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Greek nai nai, ou ou), the Lord's standard of speech.
The bare word made as binding as an oath (Matthew 5:33-37).
Emeth, Hebrew, truth, the dealing-truly that is the LORD's delight (Proverbs 12:22).
Against the doubled, shifting word—“yea and nay” (2 Corinthians 1:18).
usage: The elder kept plain speech, his bare word as good as another man's bond.
The pastor rebuked the spin that tells a technical truth to leave a false impression.
She spoke the truth in love, neither deceiving with smooth words nor wounding under cover of honesty.

pos: noun phrase (integrity in trade and labour)
etymology: From “honest” (Latin honestus, honourable) and “commerce” (Latin commercium, trade); the whole ethic of integrity in buying, selling, lending, labour, and wages.
biblical_def: Honest commerce is the whole ethic of integrity in trade, labour, lending, and wages—the lordship of God extended over the marketplace. Where the entry on just weights and measures treats the specific instrument of the balance, honest commerce names the broader duty: “If thou sell ought unto thy neighbour, or buyest ought of thy neighbour's hand, ye shall not oppress one another.” Scripture binds the conscience over the whole transaction—the truthful representation of goods, the fair price, the kept contract, the honest day's work, and above all the prompt and full payment of wages. James thunders against the employer who defrauds the labourer: “the hire of the labourers… which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.” The prophet sums the whole of it: to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God; and the wise man prizes a good name above great riches. The dictionary marks honest commerce as a matter of true religion, against two corruptions. The first severs faith from business, making a man devout on the Lord's Day and a cheat the rest of the week, as though the marketplace ran by its own rules. The second baptizes greed, treating profit as the highest good and any advantage as fair. Against both, the dictionary holds that the God who searches the heart also audits the ledger: every fraud, withheld wage, padded bill, and deceptive sale is a sin He sees and will repay, and the believer's trade is to be as honest as his prayers.
webster_summary: The whole ethic of integrity in trade, labour, lending, and wages (Leviticus 25:14; James 5:4); the lordship of God over the marketplace, against severing faith from business and against the baptizing of greed.
webster_full: HONEST COMMERCE, noun phrase. Integrity in trade, labour, lending, and wages.
“Ye shall not oppress one another” in buying and selling (Leviticus 25:14).
The wage kept back by fraud cries to the Lord of sabaoth (James 5:4).
The LORD requires us to do justly and love mercy (Micah 6:8).
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches (Proverbs 22:1).
scriptures: And if thou sell ought unto thy neighbour, or buyest ought of thy neighbour's hand, ye shall not oppress one another.
Jas 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
corruption_summary: One corruption severs faith from business, making a man devout on Sunday and a cheat all week; the other baptizes greed, treating profit as the highest good and any advantage as fair.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over the marketplace. The first corruption is the division of life into sacred and secular, so that a man is devout on the Lord's Day and a deceiver the rest of the week—the padded invoice, the withheld wage, the misrepresented goods all reckoned “just business.” Scripture knows no such division: the God who commands honest weights also forbids oppression in every sale, and the wage kept back by fraud cries in His ears. The fear of God either reaches the ledger or it is not the fear of God.

The opposite corruption baptizes greed, making profit the highest good and counting any advantage fair that the law allows. But the LORD requires us to do justly and love mercy, and prizes a good name above great riches. The dictionary recovers honest commerce as a chief field of obedience: the truthful sale, the fair price, the kept contract, the honest labour, the prompt and full wage. The God who searches the heart audits the ledger; the believer's trade is to be as honest as his prayers, and his marketplace dealings a witness to the world of the righteousness that exalteth a nation.
roots_summary: From the Latin honestus (honourable) and commercium (trade, exchange); the broad ethic of marketplace integrity, of which just weights and measures is the particular case.
roots_lines: Honestus, Latin, honourable, worthy of esteem.
Commercium, Latin, trade or exchange, the root of “commerce.”
'Osheq, Hebrew, oppression or fraud, forbidden in trade (Leviticus 25:14).
The withheld “hire” (Greek misthos) that cries to God (James 5:4).
Broader than just weights and measures, covering sale, wage, lending, and contract.
usage: The merchant kept honest commerce, his trade as truthful as his prayers.
The pastor preached that the wage withheld by fraud cries in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
She refused the padded bill, knowing the God who searches the heart audits the ledger.

etymology: From “foretell” (to predict) and “forthtell” (to declare forth); the distinction between prophecy as prediction of the future and prophecy as the bold declaration of God's word.
biblical_def: “Foretelling versus forthtelling” names the distinction between the two senses in which Scripture uses prophecy: foretelling, the prediction of things to come, and forthtelling, the bold declaration of the word of God to the present generation. The prophets did both. They foretold—the LORD does nothing but He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets—and the predictive element, fulfilled to the letter, is a chief proof of divine inspiration, for God alone declares the end from the beginning. But far more of their ministry was forthtelling: declaring the word God put in their mouths, calling the people to repentance, denouncing sin, comforting the afflicted, and pressing the claims of the covenant. The New Testament gift of prophecy is largely forthtelling in this sense—“he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.” The dictionary marks the distinction to correct two errors. The first reduces all prophecy to prediction, so that the prophet is treated as a mere fortune-teller and the prophetic books are mined only for end-times forecasts, missing their overwhelming burden of present-tense call and rebuke. The second, opposite error so emphasizes forthtelling that it denies genuine predictive prophecy altogether—the rationalist move that dates prophecies after the fact and strips Scripture of its supernatural foreknowledge. The dictionary holds both: God truly foretold the future, and His foretelling vindicates His Word; and God's prophets chiefly forthtold His will to their own age, as faithful preaching, grounded in the prophetic word, still does today.
webster_summary: The distinction between prophecy as foretelling (prediction of the future) and forthtelling (bold declaration of God's word to the present); the prophets did both, and the dictionary affirms genuine prediction while recovering the larger burden of present-tense proclamation.
webster_full: FORETELLING VS. FORTHTELLING, noun phrase. The two senses of biblical prophecy.
Foretelling: prediction of things to come, a proof of inspiration (Amos 3:7).
Forthtelling: the bold declaration of God's word to the present generation.
NT prophecy is largely forthtelling—edification, exhortation, comfort (1 Corinthians 14:3).
The prophets did both; both are grounded in the word God put in their mouths (Jeremiah 1:9).
scriptures: For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
Am 3:7
Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
Jer 1:9
Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.
corruption_summary: One error reduces prophecy to mere prediction, treating prophets as fortune-tellers; the rationalist opposite denies genuine prediction, dating prophecies after the fact to strip Scripture of supernatural foreknowledge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the full nature of biblical prophecy. One error reduces all prophecy to prediction, treating the prophets as fortune-tellers and the prophetic books as a quarry for end-times charts. This misses the overwhelming burden of their ministry, which was forthtelling—calling a covenant people to repentance, denouncing sin, comforting the afflicted, and pressing the word of God upon the present hour. The prophet was first a preacher, not a forecaster.

The opposite and graver error is the rationalist denial of genuine predictive prophecy. To escape the supernatural, critics date prophecies after the events they “predict”—Daniel to the second century, Isaiah's naming of Cyrus to a later hand. The dictionary rejects this: God truly foretold the future, declaring the end from the beginning, and the fulfilment of His predictions is a chief proof of inspiration, for He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets. The dictionary holds both senses together—real foretelling that vindicates the Word, and the larger forthtelling that faithful preaching, grounded in that Word, continues to this day.
roots_summary: From “foretell” (to predict beforehand) and “forthtell” (to declare forth); both rendering the work of the Hebrew navi' (prophet, spokesman) and Greek prophetes.
roots_lines: “Foretell,” to predict the future, the predictive sense of prophecy.
“Forthtell,” to declare forth God's word to the present.
Navi', Hebrew, a prophet, a called spokesman for God.
Prophetes, Greek, one who speaks forth (pro- + phemi) the divine word.
Both grounded in the word God puts in the prophet's mouth (Jeremiah 1:9).
usage: The teacher distinguished foretelling from forthtelling to recover the prophets' burden of present-tense call.
He defended genuine predictive prophecy against the rationalist dating of prophecies after the fact.
She saw that faithful preaching today is forthtelling, grounded in the prophetic word.

pos: noun phrase (two modes of figurative reading)
etymology: From “allegory” (Greek allegoria, speaking otherwise) and “typology” (Greek typos, a pattern or figure); the distinction between fanciful allegorizing and the God-given types of Scripture.
biblical_def: “Allegory versus typology” names the crucial distinction between two modes of figurative reading: the disciplined recognition of God-given types, and the undisciplined imposition of allegory. A type is a real person, event, or institution of the Old Testament, divinely intended to prefigure a greater New Testament reality in Christ—the passover lamb, the brazen serpent, the tabernacle, Adam as a figure of Him that was to come. Such types are grounded in genuine history and warranted by the New Testament's own interpretation; they are “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” The apostle calls the events of the wilderness “ensamples” (types) written for our admonition. Allegory, by contrast, in its undisciplined Alexandrian form, treats the literal sense as a mere husk to be discarded for hidden meanings imposed by the interpreter's fancy—finding secret significances in numbers, colours, and details the text never warrants. The dictionary marks the distinction sharply. Typology is sound: it reads forward from real history to its fulfilment in Christ, governed by the analogy of faith and the apostolic example. Undisciplined allegory is unsound: it reads meanings into the text by imagination, and once unmoored from the literal sense, any text can be made to mean anything. Paul's single use of the word “allegory” (of Hagar and Sarah) is itself a controlled, apostolically-warranted typology, not a license for fancy. The rule the dictionary commends is the Reformed one: honour the literal sense as the foundation, receive the God-given types the Scripture itself identifies, and refuse the allegorizing that finds Christ where the Spirit never placed Him.
webster_summary: The distinction between God-given types (real history prefiguring Christ, warranted by the NT) and undisciplined allegory (meanings imposed by fancy); typology reads forward from the literal sense, allegory reads meaning into it.
webster_full: ALLEGORY VS. TYPOLOGY, noun phrase. Two modes of figurative reading, the one sound, the other suspect.
A type is real history divinely intended to prefigure Christ (1 Corinthians 10:11).
Types are “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:17).
Undisciplined allegory discards the literal sense for imposed hidden meanings.
Typology reads forward from the text; allegory reads meaning into it.
scriptures: Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Heb 10:1

For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
corruption_summary: The Alexandrian habit of undisciplined allegory imposes meanings the text never warrants; the opposite error so fears allegory that it denies the genuine, God-given types the New Testament itself identifies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is disciplined, Christ-centred interpretation. The first corruption is undisciplined allegory, the Alexandrian habit following Origen: treating the literal sense as a husk to be discarded for hidden meanings the interpreter supplies—the colour of a curtain, a number in a genealogy, a detail strained past all warrant. Once unmoored from the literal sense, allegory can make any text mean anything, and Scripture becomes wax in the interpreter's hand. The dictionary refuses it.

The opposite error so fears allegory that it denies typology altogether, flattening the Old Testament into bare history with no forward witness to Christ. But the New Testament itself reads the passover, the serpent, the tabernacle, and Adam as types fulfilled in Christ, calling the wilderness events “ensamples” written for us, and the law a shadow whose body is Christ. The dictionary holds the Reformed rule: honour the literal sense as the foundation, receive the God-given types the Scripture identifies, read forward from real history to its fulfilment in Christ—and refuse the fanciful allegory that finds Christ where the Spirit never placed Him.
roots_summary: From the Greek allegoria (“speaking otherwise”) and typos (“a pattern, figure, ensample”); the one a mode of imposed figure, the other the God-intended prefiguration of Christ.
roots_lines: Allegoria, Greek, “speaking otherwise,” saying one thing to mean another.
Typos, Greek, a pattern, figure, or “ensample” (1 Corinthians 10:11).
Skia, Greek, a “shadow” of things to come, whose body is Christ (Colossians 2:17).
Paul's one use of “allegory” (Galatians 4:24) is a controlled, warranted typology.
Governed by the literal sense and the analogy of faith.
usage: The teacher distinguished the God-given type from the fanciful allegory the text never warrants.
He honoured the passover lamb as a true type while refusing to allegorize the colour of the curtains.
She read forward from real history to Christ, governed by the apostolic example.

pos: noun phrase (the civil ruler under God)
etymology: From “magistrate” (Latin magistratus, a public office); the civil ruler considered as a minister of God, accountable to rule justly and in the fear of God.
biblical_def: The Christian magistrate is the civil ruler considered as a minister of God—the office of governing authority understood in the light of Scripture, accountable to the God who ordained it. The apostle teaches that the powers that be are ordained of God, and that the ruler is the minister of God for good, bearing the sword to execute wrath upon the evildoer; rulers are therefore not autonomous but stewards under a higher King. Scripture sets the standard for the office: “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God”; and it pronounces that “righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.” The church is charged to pray for kings and all in authority, that under good government it may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. The dictionary holds the civil magistrate to be a God-ordained authority within its proper sphere, distinct from the family and the church, owed honour and obedience in all things lawful. On the harder questions—how far the magistrate should establish or defend true religion, and the proper relation of church and state—the Reformed tradition has differed, the older establishment view (and Bucer's De Regno Christi) leaning on the godly prince, while the Baptist tradition, with the 1689 Confession, stresses liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom. The dictionary marks the office against two errors: the statism that makes the government an idol owed unlimited obedience, when the magistrate is himself under God and may be disobeyed when he commands sin; and the antinomian or anarchic spirit that despises lawful authority, which Scripture commands the Christian to honour as ordained of God.
webster_summary: The civil ruler as a minister of God, ordained within his proper sphere and accountable to rule justly in the fear of God (Romans 13:1; 2 Samuel 23:3); owed honour and lawful obedience, against both statist idolatry and anarchic contempt of authority.
webster_full: CHRISTIAN MAGISTRATE, noun phrase. The civil ruler considered as a minister of God.
“The powers that be are ordained of God” (Romans 13:1).
“He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God” (2 Samuel 23:3).
The church is to pray for kings and all in authority (1 Timothy 2:2).
Owed honour and lawful obedience, yet himself under God and resistible when he commands sin.
scriptures: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me, He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.
corruption_summary: Statism makes government an idol owed unlimited obedience, forgetting the magistrate is under God; the anarchic spirit despises lawful authority Scripture commands the Christian to honour as ordained of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the magistrate as God's minister, neither an idol nor a nullity. The first corruption is statism: the making of government into a god owed unlimited and unconditional obedience. Scripture forbids this. The magistrate is ordained of God but is under God, a minister accountable to rule justly in His fear; when he commands what God forbids, the Christian must obey God rather than men. The state that claims the conscience claims what belongs to God alone.

The opposite corruption is the anarchic or antinomian contempt of authority that despises lawful rulers and counts submission beneath Christian liberty. But the apostle commands every soul to be subject to the higher powers, to honour the king, and to pray for all in authority. The dictionary holds the balance, while noting the Reformed family's long differences over the magistrate's role in religion—the older establishment view leaning on the godly prince, the Baptist tradition stressing liberty of conscience and the spiritual kingdom. On that the conscience is not here bound; but the abiding rule stands: honour the magistrate as ordained of God, obey him in all things lawful, resist him only where he commands sin, and remember that righteousness, not raw power, exalteth a nation.
roots_summary: From the Latin magistratus (a public office or officer); the civil authority considered, with Romans 13, as a diakonos (minister) of God for good.
roots_lines: Magistratus, Latin, a public office or magistrate.
Exousiai, Greek, the “higher powers” ordained of God (Romans 13:1).
Diakonos Theou, “minister of God,” the ruler's title in Romans 13:4.
The “sword” he bears for justice, distinct from the church's spiritual power.
Distinguished from family and church as a separate God-ordained sphere.
usage: The pastor taught that the magistrate is God's minister, owed honour yet himself under God.
He resisted the statism that claims the conscience, obeying God rather than men where they conflict.
She prayed for kings and all in authority, that the church might lead a quiet and peaceable life.
